period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 9 periods = 405 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 45min

periods.activity_title: First Encounter: Reading the Poem Aloud

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.17–19): summary-fill exercise using exact words from the poem.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud, students follow in their textbooks (p.17–18). Pause at each stanza to allow students to absorb the garden imagery and the comic tone established by the refrain.
Students read the poem again in pairs, taking turns stanza by stanza. Invite two or three pairs to read aloud for the class, attending to rhythm and the repeated opening line.
Work through the ‘Let us read’ summary-fill task (p.19) as a whole class. Students supply exact words from the poem for each blank and confirm answers by locating the lines in the text.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem’s light-hearted, wry tone can be lost if students rush through it; slow, expressive read-alouds help them feel the comic rhythm before analysis begins. Watch for confusion between the speaker and Reginald Arkell, the named poet — the speaker is the unnamed neighbour, not the poet himself. Students who finish early may be pointed to the appreciation note on p.18 for independent reading.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.19): multiple-choice questions on tone, speaker, and rhyme scheme.
Let us discuss (p.20): complete sentences on the word ‘stones’ and garden imagery.

time_bands.activity: Open with a brief whole-class recall: ask students what they remember of Mrs. Jones’s garden from their reading of the poem. Accept two or three responses to warm the room.

Work through the ‘Let us discuss’ multiple-choice questions on tone, speaker, and rhyme scheme (p.19). Discuss each option as a class, asking students to justify their choices with evidence from the poem.

Move to the sentence-completion task on the word ‘stones’ and garden imagery (p.20). Students choose between the bracketed options and explain their reasoning in one sentence each before recording their answers.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the poem closely, students may confuse ‘tone’ with ‘mood’; clarify that tone is the speaker’s attitude, while mood is the feeling the poem creates in the reader. The rhyme-scheme question often trips students who mark internal rhymes as scheme units; direct them to line-end sounds only. Students who are uncertain about the AABB pattern can be shown the first stanza as a model before they scan the rest.

periods.activity_title: Literary Devices: Alliteration, Refrain, and Irony

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.20): identify examples of alliteration from the poem.
Let us think and reflect (p.20): identify the refrain in the poem.
Let us think and reflect (p.20): identify the lines displaying situational irony.

time_bands.activity: Briefly introduce alliteration with one or two examples drawn from everyday life, then ask students to scan the poem and write down every pair or group of words sharing an initial sound. Pairs compare findings and the class compiles a shared list.

Introduce the term ‘refrain’ using the poem’s own opening line as the example. Students identify which line repeats across all three stanzas and discuss why the poet chose to anchor each stanza with it.

Work through the situational irony task (p.20): students locate the final couplet, explain in writing what the speaker expected versus what actually happened, and share their explanations with a partner before a short whole-class discussion.

periods.teacher_notes: Students commonly name any repeated word as alliteration rather than focusing on repeated initial consonant sounds; after identifying examples, ask them to say the words aloud so the sonic pattern becomes clear. The situational irony in the final couplet — the speaker standing on the very flower they have been searching for — is the poem’s comic climax and worth dwelling on. Those who finish the irony task early may be directed to consider how the irony changes their view of the speaker.

periods.activity_title: The Title’s Pun and Extract Analysis

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.20): complete sentences on the dual meaning of ‘concrete’ in the title.
Let us think and reflect (p.20–21): read the first-stanza extract and answer inference and true/false questions.

time_bands.activity: Ask students: “What does the word ‘concrete’ mean to you?” Collect responses, then guide them toward its two meanings — the literal stone material in Mrs. Jones’s garden and the figurative sense of ‘clear or tangible’. Students complete the two sentence-stems on p.20 in their notebooks.

Read the first-stanza extract on p.20–21 as a class. Work through the extract-analysis questions — inference on Mrs. Jones’s taste, the true/false statement about the garden revealing character, the meaning of ‘crazy path’, and the MCQ on the sundial. Students answer individually, then discuss in pairs before a whole-class share.

periods.teacher_notes: The pun in the title is the poem’s most sophisticated device and students may not spontaneously notice the figurative sense; prompt by asking whether the poem gives a ‘clear example’ of something about human nature. In the extract questions, the ‘crazy path’ item is easily misread as a literal comment on Mrs. Jones’s judgment — redirect students to the word’s older meaning of ‘irregular or winding’. Students who finish early can be pointed to the appreciation paragraph on p.18 for a self-study reading of how the imagery is analysed there.

periods.activity_title: Mrs. Jones in Depth and Listening to the Rock Garden

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.21): answer short-response questions about Mrs. Jones’s feelings, the pin image, and her character.
Let us listen (p.23): listen to the Rock Garden presentation and answer questions in one to three words.

time_bands.activity: Students work in pairs on the three short-response questions about Mrs. Jones (p.21): how she feels about her garden, why the speaker imagines a pin, and what the garden and conversation reveal about her character. Pairs share answers and the class discusses the portrait that emerges.

Transition to the listening activity. Set the context: students will hear a short presentation about the Rock Garden of Chandigarh. Teacher reads the transcript (p.47) at a measured pace while students listen with books closed.

Students answer the five ‘Let us listen’ questions on p.23 from memory, using one to three words per answer. Teacher reads the transcript a second time while students verify and complete their responses.

periods.teacher_notes: Having discussed Mrs. Jones’s eccentric passion for stones, students are primed to connect her garden to the Rock Garden of Chandigarh — a real-world celebration of stone and waste materials. The listening questions require exact words from the presentation, so caution students against paraphrasing their answers. Students who find the short-answer format difficult may benefit from hearing the transcript a third time for specific items.

periods.activity_title: The Art of Apology: Informal and Formal Register

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.23–24): role-play informal apologies for four everyday situations using given phrases.
Let us speak (p.24): role-play formal apologies to a person in authority for three school situations.

time_bands.activity: Open with the poem’s final moment: the speaker has just been told they were standing on Mrs. Jones’s cherished flower. Ask the class: what might the speaker say next? Briefly model an informal apology to show how tone and word choice differ from everyday conversation.

Pairs take turns role-playing the four informal apology situations on p.23–24, using the suggested phrases displayed on the board. After each pair, one or two groups perform for the class and receive brief peer feedback on tone and phrasing.

Shift to the formal register: pairs work through the three school-setting situations on p.24 — late submission, lateness, and missing project. Encourage students to choose from the formal phrases, respond appropriately, and then swap roles. Two or three pairs perform for the class.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently use informal phrases in the formal role-plays and vice versa; pause after each performance to highlight one successful register choice and one that could be adjusted. The poem’s comic climax — the speaker unwittingly standing on Mrs. Jones’s flower — provides a memorable anchor for why an apology is called for. Students who are hesitant to perform may be given the option to write out one exchange first before speaking it aloud.
materials: Whiteboard with phrase lists for informal and formal apology

periods.activity_title: Drafting a Formal Notice for the Herb Garden

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.25): draft a formal notice about the Herb Garden inauguration for Grades 6–8.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays a model notice on the board, labelling each structural element: organisation name, date, title, body (purpose, date, time, venue, contact), signature, class. Students identify the elements aloud and note the third-person formal register.

Students plan their notice using a brief checklist: have I included purpose, date, time, venue, contact details? They then draft the notice in a box in their notebooks, following the formal third-person format outlined on p.25.

Students exchange notebooks with a partner and use the checklist to give one specific point of praise and one suggestion. Writers revise their notices based on the feedback and the unit closes with two or three volunteers sharing their completed notices aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem’s connection to gardens makes the Herb Garden notice a thematically natural writing task; briefly drawing that link helps motivate the writing. Students commonly omit the contact-details line or forget to write in the third person; the partner-checklist step is designed to catch both errors before revision. Students who finish early may add an optional tagline to their notice that captures the spirit of the Herb Garden.
materials: Checklist on board or printed slip

periods.activity_title: Words in Context: Synonyms, Instruments, and Word-Building

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.21): select appropriate synonym replacements for four underlined words from the poem.
Let us learn (p.22): match five types of instruments in Column 1 with definitions in Column 2.
Let us learn (p.22–23): replace first letters of ‘nice’ and ‘soil’ to build new words from clues.

time_bands.activity: Students work on the synonym-replacement task (p.21): for each of the four underlined words from the poem — ‘strange’, ‘nice’, ‘delicate’, ‘cried’ — they read the options, return to the poem line for context, and select the most fitting replacement. Brief class discussion confirms choices.

Introduce the instrument-matching task (p.22) by asking students to infer the meaning of ‘device’ from the poem. Students then match the five instrument types — implement, tool, equipment, appliance, gadget — to their definitions and add further examples to Column 3.

Students tackle the word-building activity (p.22–23): replacing the first letter of ‘nice’ and ‘soil’ to create new words from meaning clues. Pairs race to complete both sets, then the class checks answers together.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the poem carefully, students have already encountered ‘strange’, ‘nice’, ‘delicate’ and ‘cried’ in context, which makes the synonym task a genuine exercise in contextual nuance rather than guesswork. The instrument-matching task rewards careful reading of definitions; students often conflate ‘tool’ and ‘implement’ — ask them to think of what a hammer does versus what a cricket bat is used for. The word-building game with ‘nice’ and ‘soil’ works well as a quick pair competition.

periods.activity_title: Gardens, Creativity, and the World Beyond the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.25–26): research a popular garden in your region and prepare a short presentation for the class.

homework.task_brief: Let us explore (p.26): collect fallen flowers and leaves at home to create a pressed-flower artwork over the coming days.

time_bands.activity: Open with a synthesis discussion: invite students to name what Mrs. Jones’s stone garden, the Rock Garden of Chandigarh, and Amrit Udyan in New Delhi have in common. Draw out the idea that each turns ordinary or unusual material into something valued and beautiful.

In small groups, students pool what they know (or quickly note) about a garden in their own region. Each group frames three talking points: the garden’s distinctive feature, what materials or plants it is known for, and why it matters to the community. Groups draft a brief spoken presentation outline.

Groups take turns delivering their short presentation to the class — one to two minutes each. Listeners note one thing they found surprising. The unit closes with the teacher drawing together the chapter’s central idea: that paying close attention — as Mrs. Jones does, as Nek Chand did — reveals extraordinary things in the ordinary world.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit draws together the poem’s comic portrait of Mrs. Jones, the listening text on the Rock Garden, and the garden-writing task: all three involve finding value in stones, plants, and overlooked materials. Students who are unfamiliar with local gardens can describe a park or any green space they know; the point is the reflective act of observing a place carefully. The pressed-flower homework on p.26 is set as a take-home creative task that does not affect the unit’s in-class work.
materials: Any reference materials students bring about local gardens

items.source_context: Tone, rhyme scheme, alliteration, refrain, situational irony, title pun, extract analysis of Mrs. Jones’s stone garden.
items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 17 beginning “My next-door neighbour, Mrs. Jones.” Which of the following best describes the overall tone of the poem?

options.label: A
options.text: Bitter and resentful, showing the speaker’s deep dislike of Mrs. Jones.

options.label: B
options.text: Formal and instructive, explaining the correct way to maintain a stone garden.

options.label: C
options.text: Gentle and wryly amused, presenting Mrs. Jones’s garden habits with warm humour.

options.label: D
options.text: Sorrowful and nostalgic, mourning the loss of a beautiful garden.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Students who choose this misread the speaker’s bemused detachment as hostility toward Mrs. Jones.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests a confusion between a sad subject and a sorrowful tone; the poem’s comic rhythm signals amusement, not loss.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Reflects a misreading of the poem as informational rather than as a light-hearted character sketch.

items.source_lo: Student reads and responds to a poem using close reading of language, tone, literary devices, and the poem’s overall effect as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Tone, rhyme scheme, alliteration, refrain, situational irony, title pun, extract analysis of Mrs. Jones’s stone garden.
items.item_stem: The poem ends with Mrs. Jones telling the speaker “You’re standing on it.” Explain in two or three sentences how this moment creates situational irony, and what it reveals about the difference between the speaker’s perspective and Mrs. Jones’s.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The situational irony arises because the speaker has spent a quarter of an hour asking where the cherished flower is, only to discover they have been crushing it underfoot the entire time. This gap between what the speaker expected — to be shown something visible and prominent — and what actually happened reveals that Mrs. Jones notices and treasures things so small and close to the ground that a casual observer literally overlooks them.

items.source_context: Rock Garden of Chandigarh: Nek Chand, 40 acres, postage stamp, Padma Shri, three phases, waste-material sculptures, 5000 statues.
items.item_stem: Listen to the presentation about the Rock Garden of Chandigarh. Which of the following statements about the Rock Garden is true according to the presentation?

options.label: A
options.text: The borders of the Rock Garden are lined with approximately 500 statues.

options.label: B
options.text: The Rock Garden is divided into five distinct phases, each with a different theme.

options.label: C
options.text: The Rock Garden was created by Nek Chand in 1957 and covers 40 acres.

options.label: D
options.text: The Rock Garden was created in 1983 and featured on a postage stamp a year later.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Students who choose this confuse the year of creation (1957) with the postage-stamp year (1983).
what_each_option_reveals.B: Reflects a mishearing or misremembering; the presentation states three distinct phases, not five.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Students who choose this have confused the approximate figure; the presentation states around 5,000 statues.

items.source_context: Rock Garden of Chandigarh: Nek Chand, 40 acres, postage stamp, Padma Shri, three phases, waste-material sculptures, 5000 statues.
items.item_stem: After listening to the presentation, a student says: “The Rock Garden is just a normal outdoor sculpture park built from new materials.” Write two to three sentences explaining why this statement is inaccurate, using specific details from the presentation.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The statement is inaccurate because the Rock Garden was built using waste materials — including broken toilet pots, terracotta pots, and light fixtures — transformed into sculptures and mosaic art pieces. It is not an ordinary outdoor park but a 40-acre installation divided into three distinct phases celebrating creativity from discarded objects.

items.item_stem: Your friend lent you their favourite book and you accidentally left it on the school bus. Role-play the conversation in which you apologise to your friend. Use at least two appropriate informal phrases and show how your friend responds.

expected_elements: Uses at least two informal apology phrases naturally and correctly.
Acknowledges the specific mistake clearly in the apology.
Partner’s response is appropriate and in informal register.
Tone is sincere rather than stiff or overly formal.

items.source_lo: Student uses role-play to practise expressing apologies in both informal and formal registers as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Informal apologies to friends and family; formal apologies to a teacher or principal in school situations.
items.item_stem: You are a student who forgot to submit an important assignment. Your teacher has asked you to explain. Role-play the conversation: apologise formally, offer a reason, and suggest how you will make sure it does not happen again. Your partner plays the teacher and responds in a formal register.

expected_elements: Uses formal apology phrases and maintains formal register throughout.
Gives a credible reason for the lapse without making excuses.
Proposes a concrete remedy or assurance to the teacher.
Teacher’s response (by partner) is appropriately formal and constructive.

items.item_stem: You are the Secretary of the Eco Club of your school. Draft a formal notice for students of Grades 6 to 8 announcing a Tree Plantation Drive to be held in the school grounds. Include: the organisation’s name, the date on which the notice is issued, a clear title, the body (purpose of the drive, date, time, venue, whom to contact), and your name with designation. Write the notice in a box and use formal third-person language.

expected_elements: Notice is written inside a box with all structural elements present.
Third-person formal language used consistently throughout.
Body includes purpose, date, time, venue, and contact details.
Name and designation of the issuing student are clearly stated.

items.item_stem: Imagine you are on the editorial board of your school magazine. Write a short opinion piece (one paragraph, approximately 80 words) arguing why every school should have a garden — like the Herb Garden described in the chapter — and what students could learn from tending it. Use formal written English.

expected_elements: States a clear opinion on why a school garden is valuable.
Gives at least two specific reasons or benefits for students.
Connects to observation or care of nature in a meaningful way.
Maintains formal written register appropriate for a school magazine.

items.item_stem: The poem describes Mrs. Jones’s sundial as a ‘device’. Choose ONE of the words below — implement, tool, appliance, gadget — and write two sentences: the first using it correctly in a sentence about something from Mrs. Jones’s garden or home, the second explaining in your own words why that word fits better than ‘device’ in that context.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Accept any response that uses the chosen word correctly in a garden or household context and gives a plausible reason why it fits better than ‘device’ (for example, ‘tool’ suggests something hand-held and purposeful, while ‘device’ is more neutral). The key criterion is that the explanation shows the student understands the semantic distinction between the two words.

items.item_stem: Choose a well-known garden, park, or green space in your region. Write a short account (four to six sentences) that describes: (a) what the place is known for, (b) one unusual or distinctive feature it has, and (c) what a visitor can learn or experience there. Share your account with the class.

expected_elements: Names a specific real garden or green space in the student’s region.
Describes at least one distinctive or unusual feature clearly.
States what a visitor can observe, learn, or experience there.
Account is four to six sentences and written in complete sentences.

items.item_stem: The poem shows that Mrs. Jones sees extraordinary beauty in stones and tiny plants that her neighbour overlooks entirely. The Rock Garden of Chandigarh turns broken pots and waste into celebrated art. Design a mini-project: identify one discarded or overlooked object or material in your neighbourhood and describe (in a plan of eight to ten sentences) how you would transform it into something useful or beautiful. Explain what the transformation would show others about paying closer attention to the world around them.

expected_elements: Identifies a specific discarded or overlooked object or material.
Describes a realistic and creative plan for transformation.
Connects the transformation to the idea of finding value in the ordinary.
Plan is eight to ten sentences with a clear sequence of steps.
